I drive the Route 9 bus and write poems on my breaks. This is from the last run of the night. What do you think?
Route 9, final run. The bus exhales.
Rows of seats keep the shapes of strangers,
a dent here, a warmth there,
and I drive the empty ghosts back to the depot
with my headlights on for them.

I spent twelve years as a paralegal and I'm opening a cafe across from the county courthouse. The name: "Grounds for Appeal." Lawyers and jurors will be my main customers. Does it work for you, or would you change anything?

I'm a retired schoolteacher and volunteer for our branch library. Here's how my fundraising letter opens: "Dear neighbor, In 1952 the Alder Street Library had 3,000 books and one stove. Today it has 11,000 books and the same stove. We are asking you to help us buy a new one, and, while we're at it, a roof." Any thoughts?
Hello, I'm a baker and just opened a sourdough place in my town. I'm putting this on the paper bags: "Three days to make. Ten minutes to vanish." Could you tell me your opinion?

Long-time fantasy reader, first-time writer here. My novel begins: "Tuesday was the day Thornwick hid its children, so the dragon's tax collector found only goats, a very old man, and an unusually loud silence." Would you tell me what you think? Be gentle, I'm a bit anxious about this.

I'm a junior in chemistry and I'm putting together a pitch for a competition. Here's my one sentence: "Universities auction off decommissioned lab equipment for pennies, so we recondition and calibrate it, certify it, and sell forty-year-old spectrometers to high school and community college labs at a tenth of the price of new." Any feedback?

I teach high school drama and I'm writing a musical about a stagehand. This is her big chorus:
Somebody's got to stand in the dark
So the star can find her mark
I'm the tape on the floor, the ghost light's spark
I'm the reason you won't fall
And I'm not in the program at all
I'd love your opinion before I show the cast.

I'm 67 and marrying for the second time, after being widowed. My toast: "Thirty years ago I promised someone forever and meant it. Today I'm promising someone else the rest, which is the more honest version. Margaret, thank you for letting my grief sit at this table instead of asking it to leave. To those who aren't here, and to those who are." Does it feel right to you?

units:
I teach bike repair as a hobby and want to run a workshop at the shop where I work. Pitching my manager:
"Hi Gus, what about a free 'Fix Your Own Flat' class, Saturdays at 10, six people max? We'd supply two spare tubes each, which cost us about $4, and attendees tend to buy levers and patch kits afterward. I'd teach it on my own time. Can we try one in April? Thanks, Wren"
What do you think?

Here's the opening line of my historical novel, set in 1880s Hungary: "The year the river changed its mind, my father sold our cow, our name, and nearly me." I'm a history student and I've been staring at this one for ages. Any feedback would be welcome.

I'm applying for a historical marker for the old Delmar Bakery on 5th Street. Our statement opens: "For 41 years this building fed the neighborhood on credit. A ledger still hangs on the back wall, recording striking miners' debts the owner never collected. Towns are remembered for their monuments, but they're held together by their bakeries." How does it read to you?

I run a pottery studio and I'm starting a scholarship fund for teens. The letter opens: "Clay doesn't care about your grades. It doesn't care who your parents are, or whether you've eaten today. It only cares whether you're paying attention. We'd like to offer fifteen teenagers a seat at the wheel, free, for a year." How does it read to you?

I'm 19 and write stories in my notes app on the bus. Here's the start of one, I'm kind of curious what you'd say: "My brother says the moon follows our car because it's lonely. I say it follows because Dad drives slow. Either way, by the time we reached Aunt Dee's, it had parked itself over the chicken coop, and the whole backseat had agreed not to mention that Mom was crying."

I'm a farmer, new to writing. In the town of Marl, your umbrella opens onto whatever you're feeling: Grandpa's makes drizzle, the mayor's makes hail. Nell's opens only sunshine, because she never lets anyone see her sad. The day it finally drizzles over her, the whole town comes to stand underneath. Tell me what you think, please.

I'm opening a chess café named En Passant. The logo is a pawn in solid black, front-on. But its round head is a coffee cup seen from above: a ring, dark liquid inside, and a small handle at the right side where a pawn would have nothing. Everything else is perfectly standard. I'd like your opinion, please.

I'm a nursing student, and I was asked to say a few words for Carol, a night-shift nurse retiring after 38 years: "Carol taught me that 3 a.m. is when patients tell the truth. Hold the hand, she said, lower the lights, and wait. Thirty-eight years of waiting with strangers so they weren't alone. I may never be as good, but I'll be awake, and that was the first thing she taught me." Honest opinion?

Hi! For my nursing capstone I came up with this: "Among night-shift nurses on medical-surgical wards, does a protected 20-minute nap during breaks reduce medication administration errors in the final three hours of shift compared with caffeine alone?" I'm a bit nervous about showing my advisor. Thoughts?

Food truck owner here, and this is my salsa macha: toast 1 cup peanuts, 3 tbsp sesame seeds, and 6 chiles de árbol and 4 guajillos in 1 cup of neutral oil on low until fragrant and just darkening. Cool, then add 4 cloves roasted garlic, 1 tbsp piloncillo, 1 tsp dried orange peel, 1 tbsp cider vinegar and salt. Pulse it chunky. It goes on everything. Thoughts?

units:
I'm a 45-year-old accountant who just started a punk band with two friends from the office. Our chorus:
I carry the one, I carry the two
Carry your lunch order, carry the blame
Tonight I'm carrying nothing but a guitar
And my own goddamn name
What's your take? Please be straight with me.

I'm a taxi driver, 40, and I moved here eleven years ago. I've been turning my feelings into songs. This is the chorus of the newest:
I wear two watches, one for here, one for home
One says it's noon, one says you're asleep
I live in the hours that don't have a name
Keeping time for the ones I can't keep
I'd be grateful for your opinion.

I run a true-crime podcast as a hobby and wrote an essay about the genre. Thesis: "True-crime podcasts promise justice but deliver intimacy: the genre's appeal lies less in solving cases than in the feeling of being trusted with a stranger's worst day, one episode at a time." What do you think?

I'm a 62-year-old dairy farmer. At my neighbor Walt's retirement, I said: 'Walt farmed the same hundred and sixty acres as his father. People call that standing still. But I watched him walk that fence line every morning for forty years, and the ground under him changed more than any of us did. You don't stay in one place by not moving. You stay by tending.' Honest feedback welcome.

I'm a literary translator replying to a post claiming AI will make us obsolete: "Translation isn't swapping words. It's deciding what to lose. Every sentence of Chekhov costs something in English, and someone has to choose the price. A machine can hand you the menu. It can't tell you which dish to give up, or sit with you while you grieve it." Posting this tonight. Would you share it?

Nurse of 11 years trying to move into UX research. Here's my pitch paragraph, please be straight with me: "I have run roughly 40,000 usability tests, though we called them shifts. I know exactly where your charting software fails: 3 a.m., one hand gloved, during a rapid response. I can't yet build a Figma prototype as polished as yours, but I can tell you which button a frightened person will press first." What do you think?

Here's my thesis for my music studies seminar, would appreciate your feedback: "Hip-hop sampling is best understood not as theft or homage but as citation: producers like J Dilla built arguments out of other records the way scholars build them out of footnotes." Where would you push me next?

As a new mom going back to school, I'm writing about lullabies. My thesis: "Lullabies across cultures are strikingly dark, with falling cradles and wolves at the door, because they soothe not through content but by letting the parent perform her own anxiety for the infant in a safe, rhythmic, controlled form." I'd love to hear what you think.

Nursing student here, working on a startup idea for my entrepreneurship elective. The pitch: "Night-shift nurses lose about twenty minutes per shift re-explaining patients at handoff, so we turn a 90-second spoken summary into a structured SBAR note that the incoming nurse approves with one tap." What's your opinion?

units:
I own a tiny skate shop and I'm not great at talking about myself, but here's my attempt. What do you think?
"I sell skateboards to teenagers and have been told 'that's cringe' by every one of them. I'm 31, I still eat it on ledges, and I keep a first aid kit in my truck for exactly that reason. Looking for someone who'll film my attempts and not post the bad ones."

We run a small vegetable farm with a CSA of 60 members. My idea: members can swap items in their box until Wednesday night, like trading kale for extra carrots. The app then sends us a harvest list adjusted by swaps, so we pick what's wanted. It also shows a 'surplus' list for cheap add-ons. Could you tell me what you think?

I'm a vegan and only a year into cooking. These are king oyster "scallops": cut stems into 2 cm thick rounds, score the tops in a crosshatch, and sear in a dry cast iron pan with a weight on top until deep brown. Then add olive oil and white miso whisked with lemon, and baste for 1 minute. Serve on pea purée with chive oil. How does it sound to you?

After 30 years as a newspaper reporter, I'm opening a cafe in the old Gazette building, and I'm calling it "Stop Press." The menu will be printed on broadsheet and the coffee will be strong enough to meet a deadline. Does the name have the right ring to it? Tell me straight, I've had worse feedback from editors.

Retired baker, still experimenting. Rye and caraway sourdough discard crackers: 150g discard, 60g rye flour, 40g olive oil, 1 tsp salt, 1 tsp caraway seeds. Mix, rest 30 minutes, roll paper thin, brush with water, and sprinkle with flaky salt and more seeds. Bake at 180°C for 18 minutes, rotating once, until they're deep amber and snap. I'd like a second opinion, please.

Philosophy grad student here. Here's my thesis for a seminar paper: "The trolley problem endures not because it reveals our moral intuitions but because it strips away the substance of moral life, relationships of prior obligation, so its answers describe only how people behave toward strangers they will never meet." Where would you push on it?

I'm 71 and I knit blankets to sell at the craft fair. My granddaughter told me to ask people online for opinions. This is my tag:
"Merino cot blanket, knitted in honeycomb stitch, which holds warmth without weight. Washed in lanolin so it stays soft. Nine evenings of work. Machine washable on the wool cycle, and made to be handed down: the edges are bound twice, because babies are hard on everything."
Does it work?

I drive long-haul and write on my phone at truck stops. Just finished the start of a blog post, "Weigh Station Poetry." It goes: "Between Amarillo and nowhere, the CB starts to sound like a congregation, forty strangers trading weather and warnings in a language none of us admitted we were inventing." Tell me what you make of it?

I teach Spanish at a high school and I'm writing a magical realism novel. First line: "In Villa Seca it rained only on people who were about to lie, which made the elections very short and the weddings very wet." Would love your feedback on it.

Here's the central question of my philosophy dissertation: "If moral testimony is epistemically legitimate in some domains, what explains why deferring to an expert about whether to donate seems acceptable while deferring about whether to forgive does not?" I'd appreciate your feedback.

units: I'm a tenant rights lawyer and my firm is Threshold. The mark is a small house silhouette sitting on a long horizontal line. Below the line, the house's reflection is not a house but a key: the roof becomes the key's bow, the chimney becomes one of its teeth. Charcoal above the line, brass below it. I'd appreciate your honest view.
I'm 10 and I made up a joke for my class talent show. What did the clock say when it got sent to the principal? "I was only tocking." My mum says I should ask someone else. What do you think?

I own a small bakery and I'm writing a post to explain our prices. Title: "Why Our Croissants Cost $4.50." First sentence: "A croissant is three days of waiting disguised as breakfast: one day for the dough, one for the butter to settle into it, and one for me to stop touching it." Could you tell me your impressions?

I run a one-item dumpling food truck and I'm pitching to a festival committee next week. Here's how I'm starting: "My truck sells exactly one thing, a dumpling, and in the next ten minutes I'm going to convince you that's a strategy and not a limitation." Can you tell me your opinion?

Just a casual share from a night-shift security guard who writes screenplays on his breaks: "Three octogenarian sisters plan to steal their late father's violin back from the museum that bought it from a forger, but the only one who can authenticate it is the sister who hasn't spoken to them in thirty years." Opinions?

Just graduated and applying for backend jobs. This is the first bullet under my internship: "Reduced p95 checkout API latency from 1.8s to 310ms by replacing N+1 Postgres queries with batched lookups and adding a read-through Redis cache, saving an estimated $42K/yr in compute." What do you think? Anything you'd change?

I'm 65 and just retired after 40 years as a high school band director. At my party I said: 'Forty years of teenagers, and I've heard every wrong note a human can play. I miss none of them. I miss all of them. Please don't clap on one and three. And if you must cry, do it in tempo.' Casually curious how that works on paper.

I'm a literary translator replying to a post claiming AI will make us obsolete: "Translation isn't swapping words. It's deciding what to lose. Every sentence of Chekhov costs something in English, and someone has to choose the price. A machine can hand you the menu. It can't tell you which dish to give up, or sit with you while you grieve it." Posting this tonight. Would you share it?

Casual question: I'm 45, sit at a desk nine hours a day, and my shoulders are creeping forward. Mon/Thu: rows, face pulls, wall angels, dead bugs. Tue/Fri: hip flexor stretch, glute bridges, goblet squats, 20-minute walk. Wed: swim or bike, whatever. Weekend: one hike. Plus a 2-minute doorway chest stretch every time my coffee finishes. Does this make sense? Roast me if needed.

I'm the mayor of a town of 6,000 and I'm campaigning for the library levy. Here's a section of my speech: "A library is the last place in town where you can walk in with no money and nobody asks why you're there. It costs the average household $41 a year. Ask yourself what else you can buy that's open to everyone, including the person you'd never think of." How does that sit with you?

units: I'm a finish carpenter applying for a set builder job at a theater. Wrote this: "Furniture is built to last fifty years. A set is built to look like it will, for six weeks, and then be burned. I find that freeing. I can fake a hundred-year-old oak door from luan and one can of walnut stain, and I can make it survive a slammed exit every night." Does that work, do you think?

I'm a junior copywriter, and this is my first pitch to a real client, a family-owned hearing-aid clinic. My line: "Hear the kettle again. The rain. Your granddaughter's whisper." Nervous to show it. How does it come across?

I'm 33, a software engineer, with a 50 km mountain race in October, and I live somewhere flat. Mon: 1 hour treadmill at 12% incline. Tue: eccentric step-ups with a 10 kg pack, 5x12 per leg. Wed: 8 km easy. Thu: parking-garage stair repeats, 6x10 floors. Fri: rest. Sat: 3-hour trail run, eating every 30 minutes as practice. Sun: 60-minute poles hike. Thoughts?

I'm launching a green burial company called Return. The symbol is a single leaf, outlined, whose veins branch out in the closed concentric whorls of a fingerprint, so the leaf also reads as a human thumbprint. Deep moss green, slightly uneven line, like it was pressed in ink. Name below in a quiet serif. I'm hoping you can give me an honest response.

I'm a physics PhD student and this is my first conference talk, so I'm nervous. I'm opening with: "If the sun were a grapefruit on this lectern, the nearest other grapefruit would be about 2,900 kilometres away, and the space between would hold, on average, nothing." What's your reaction?

i'm in 8th grade and my teacher said to pick a problem at our school. my thesis is: "Our cafeteria throws away about forty pounds of untouched food daily, and the cause isn't picky eaters but a twenty-minute lunch period that ends before students finish, so lunch should be lengthened before any composting program is considered." what do you think?

I'm a night-shift nurse, eleven years in, and I've finally started writing. Here's a title and opening line for my first post: "What the Night Shift Knows About Silence." "At 3:40 a.m. the hospital hums in B-flat, and after eleven years I can tell from a change in that hum which floor is about to have a bad hour." I'd really appreciate your feedback.

I'm a bassist who's been touring for ten years and this has happened to me twice. "When a band's player gets sick the night before a gig, we get a vetted session musician who has already studied their charts and setlist into the van within twelve hours." What do you think?
My coffee cart outside the train station needs a chalkboard line. I wrote: "Dark roast, bright side." Would you say it fits a morning commuter crowd? Let me know what you think!

Monthly cohort retention for our subscription app. I'm a data scientist and wrote it in one sitting, so tell me if I've missed something.
WITH f AS (
  SELECT customer_id, MIN(date_trunc('month', ordered_at)) AS cohort
  FROM orders GROUP BY 1)
SELECT f.cohort,
  DATEDIFF('month', f.cohort, date_trunc('month', o.ordered_at)) AS months_since,

FROM f JOIN orders o USING (customer_id)

I'm a freelance designer and invoice clients in installments. This shows what each client still owes. I aggregated billed and paid separately first so the joins don't multiply rows:
WITH b AS (SELECT client_id, SUM(amount) AS billed FROM invoices GROUP BY 1),
p AS (SELECT i.client_id, SUM(pay.amount) AS paid FROM payments pay JOIN invoices i ON i.id = pay.invoice_id GROUP BY 1)
SELECT c.name, COALESCE(b.billed, 0) - COALESCE(p.paid, 0) AS owed
FROM clients c LEFT JOIN b ON b.client_id = c.id LEFT JOIN p ON p.client_id = c.id
ORDER BY owed DESC;
Thoughts?

```python
def atomic_write(path, data):
    d = os.path.dirname(os.path.abspath(path))
    fd, tmp = tempfile.mkstemp(dir=d)
    try:
        with os.fdopen(fd, "w") as f:
            f.write(data)
            f.flush()
            os.fsync(f.fileno())
        os.replace(tmp, path)

        raise
```

I garden on an allotment and wrote this to decide whether to water, with recent rain counting for more. Rough hobby code, but I'd like an opinion:
```python
def needs_water(rain_mm, threshold=15, decay=0.7):
    """rain_mm is oldest-first, one value per day."""
    effective = sum(mm * decay**age
                    for age, mm in enumerate(reversed(rain_mm)))
    return effective < threshold
```
